clue.text: Stay with boy to include day in France

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it inside, so the boy's word wraps around the French day

parts.note: a boy as someone's child
the French word for day

explanation.surface: Someone books a stay with their son, making sure to include a day trip to France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Day in France' asks for the French word, not a place or date.
explanation.definitionFit: A sojourn is a temporary visit somewhere, so it is a noun synonym for a stay.

clue.text: Fibre for rope mats is a leaf extract

indicators.note: an extract is a piece taken out of something larger, so the letters are drawn from inside the words

parts.note: the letters run across mats, is, a and leaf

explanation.surface: A rope fibre used for mats is said to be extracted from a plant leaf.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, sisal really is drawn from the leaves of an agave and used for matting.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisal is the stiff fibre from an agave plant, widely used for making rope and twine.

clue.text: Chum regularly improvised music outside with me in hot tub

indicators.note: outside means the music word goes around the chum letters

parts.note: jazz is music built on improvisation

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of chum is used

parts.note: the first and third letters
me as the speaker is I

explanation.surface: A friend regularly plays improvised music outside while the speaker relaxes in a hot tub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' here keeps alternate letters starting from the first.
explanation.definitionFit: A Jacuzzi is a brand of whirlpool bath, now the general word for a bubbling hot tub.

clue.text: Second-hand American edition

parts.note: US is the United States
ed is the abbreviation for edition

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a description of a pre-owned American book.
explanation.definitionFit: Used goods have had a previous owner, so the adjective means pre-owned or not new.

clue.text: Issue over family with poorly disposed money's not a problem for me

indicators.note: in a down clue over means turned upside down, so the issue word is read backwards

parts.note: a person's issue is their offspring

indicators.note: disposed means arranged or set out, so the letters of money's are laid out afresh

parts.note: kin are one's family
feeling off means feeling unwell
taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A family dispute over a sick relative leaves someone unbothered because their own money is sorted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' looks like a matter in dispute, but it means offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is said when something does not bother or affect the speaker at all.

clue.text: Cheer try before catch is reviewed

parts.note: a judge will try, or hear, a case in court

indicators.note: something reviewed is looked back over, so the word for catch is read from its end to its start

parts.note: to net a fish is to catch it

explanation.surface: A rugby fan cheers a try scored just before a dropped catch is checked on video replay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try' looks like a rugby score, but it is the legal sense of judging a case in court.
explanation.definitionFit: To hearten someone is to encourage them and lift their spirits, a verb synonym for cheer.

clue.text: Tales of woe when fortune's dividing solid Conservatives

indicators.note: dividing means splitting something apart, so fortune's word sits between the two halves

parts.note: solid means hard
luck is fortune, with the 's supplying the S
Tories are members of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Diehard Tories split by a reversal of fortune swap stories of their misery.
explanation.walkthrough: Hard Tories are the right wing of Britain's Conservative Party; the possessive on fortune's supplies an extra letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard-luck stories are accounts of misfortune told to win sympathy, so they are tales of woe.

clue.text: Normally a second inspection secures uranium

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so the inspection word wraps around the uranium

parts.note: taken as written
s is the abbreviation for second
a perusal is a careful reading or inspection
U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: As is routine, a follow-up inspection locks away the uranium at a nuclear site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' is the time unit, abbreviated as a single letter, not an ordinal.
explanation.definitionFit: As per usual is an informal idiom meaning as always happens, so routinely or normally.

clue.text: Thrash lightweight after first of two rounds

indicators.note: first of picks the opening letter of each of the next two words

parts.note: the opening letters of two and rounds
an ounce is a very small weight

explanation.surface: A boxer gives a lightweight opponent a beating after the first two rounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First of two rounds' looks like a boxing count, but it takes the initials of both two and rounds.
explanation.definitionFit: To trounce is to defeat heavily or beat soundly, a verb synonym for thrash.

clue.text: Choose to adopt girl after partner's lack of care

parts.note: in bridge North is South's partner, abbreviated N

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in, so the choose word takes the girl letter inside it

parts.note: to elect is to choose
G is an abbreviation for girl

explanation.surface: A couple choose to adopt a girl after the partner's neglect of her came to light.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge the four players are North, South, East and West, so a partner can be N, S, E or W; G goes after the first E of ELECT.
explanation.definitionFit: Neglect is the failure to look after someone or something properly, a noun meaning lack of care.

clue.text: Next in line for gold on back of victory

indicators.note: placed on the back of something means attached after it, so the gold follows the victory word

parts.note: a victory is a success
OR is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: An athlete earns a gold medal on the back of a victory, putting them next in line for glory.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is the heraldic word for gold, a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: A successor is the person who follows on in a role or title, the heir waiting to take over.

clue.text: Papa's in error ignoring wife's point

parts.note: P is Papa in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: ignoring something leaves it out, so the wife's letter is dropped from the error word

parts.note: an error is a wrong
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: Dad has got it wrong, ignoring his wife's point in an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' looks like the wife's argument, but it is the definition: a sharp tip.
explanation.definitionFit: A prong is a sharp spike, such as one tine of a fork, so it is a pointed tip.

clue.text: Slow to get moving having left street map back in city

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left
an A-Z is a British street atlas of a city

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, so only the closing letter of city is kept

parts.note: the final letter of city

explanation.surface: A tourist is slow to set off, having left the street map back at the hotel in the city.
explanation.walkthrough: An A-Z is the standard British book of street maps for a town, named for its index running from A to Z.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lazy is idle and reluctant to make an effort, so slow to get going.

clue.text: Search mountains for somewhere to practise shooting

parts.note: to rifle through drawers is to search them
a range is a chain of mountains

explanation.surface: Hunters search the mountains for a good place to practise their shooting.
explanation.definitionFit: A rifle range is a designated ground with targets where people practise firing guns.

clue.text: Met friends having liaised to come out after football's first half

indicators.note: the first half of a word keeps its opening portion and drops the remainder

parts.note: soccer is association football

indicators.note: to come out differently suggests the letters of liaised emerge in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Players met up with friends after liaising to go out once the first half of a football match was over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First half' looks like part of a match, but it trims SOCCER to SOC.
explanation.definitionFit: To socialise is to mix with other people for pleasure, so socialised means spent time with friends.

clue.text: Way of working in ink transformed old robe

indicators.note: in places the way of working inside the reshuffled ink letters
transformed means changed in form, so the letters of ink are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
MO is modus operandi, Latin for a way of working
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: An artist's method of working ink is used to transform an old robe with new designs.
explanation.walkthrough: Modus operandi is Latin for method of working, usually shortened to its initials.
explanation.definitionFit: A kimono is the long, wide-sleeved traditional Japanese garment, an example of a robe.

clue.text: Commanding officer taking short nap after lunch is most comfortable

indicators.note: something cut short loses its end, so the nap word drops its final letter

parts.note: CO is the standard abbreviation for commanding officer
a siesta is an afternoon nap

explanation.surface: The commanding officer finds a brief doze after lunch the most comfortable part of his day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After lunch' belongs to the nap, describing the Spanish afternoon rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Cosiest is the superlative of cosy, meaning snuggest and warmest, so the most comfortable.

clue.text: Trendy lawyer's to sum up

parts.note: something in is fashionable
a brief is British slang for a barrister or solicitor

explanation.surface: A fashionable lawyer is about to give the jury a closing summary.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a lawyer is informally called a brief, after the document of instructions they receive.
explanation.definitionFit: In brief is an idiom meaning in short, briefly stated, which is what a summary does.

clue.text: At home, might be running things

parts.note: at home means in
might is power or strength

explanation.surface: Someone at home wonders whether they might soon be in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might' looks like a verb of possibility, but it is the noun meaning strength.
explanation.definitionFit: A party in power holds office and governs, so it is the one in charge of things.

clue.text: Crazy colourful scarves daughter's chucked out

indicators.note: something chucked out is thrown away, so the daughter letter is removed from the scarves word

parts.note: bandanas are brightly patterned neckerchiefs
d is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A mother goes mad because her daughter has thrown out some bright scarves.
explanation.walkthrough: BANDANAS loses its D to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Going bananas is slang for going mad, so the word is an informal adjective for crazy.

clue.text: Quiet religious house reportedly in poor condition

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard said, so the religious house is taken for its sound

parts.note: an abbey is a monastery or convent

explanation.surface: A silent monastery is said to be falling into disrepair.
explanation.definitionFit: Shabby describes something worn, faded and run-down through long use or neglect.

clue.text: Criminal in trouble, run in by US city's Republican leader

indicators.note: run in by is read as run taken inside, so the trouble word holds the running letter

parts.note: to bug someone is to trouble them
r is the cricket abbreviation for run
LA is Los Angeles

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter, so only the first letter of Republican is kept

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: A criminal in trouble is arrested by a Republican leader of an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run in' looks like slang for arrest, but here R is put inside BUG to make BURG.
explanation.definitionFit: A burglar is a criminal who breaks into buildings to steal, a specific kind of offender.

clue.text: Fouls aplenty and fight lead to sin bin

indicators.note: to foul up is to make a mess of things, so the letters of aplenty are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
to box is to fight with fists

explanation.surface: Plenty of fouls and a brawl land a hockey player in the sin bin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fouls' looks like the sporting noun, but it is a verb meaning messes up the following word.
explanation.definitionFit: In ice hockey the penalty box is the enclosure where an offending player serves time, nicknamed the sin bin.

clue.text: Nudge sheep's behind with stick

indicators.note: a behind is the rear end, so only the final letter of sheep is used

parts.note: the last letter of sheep
a rod is a stick

explanation.surface: A shepherd pokes a sheep's rear with a stick to move it along.
explanation.definitionFit: To prod is to poke or push someone gently, a verb synonym for nudge.

clue.text: Fear old man's about to be imprisoned

indicators.note: something imprisoned is locked inside, so the about word goes within the old man word

parts.note: one's old man is one's father
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: Someone fears that their father is about to be sent to prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is not a time word here but the Latin-derived abbreviation meaning concerning.
explanation.definitionFit: Dread is great fear or apprehension, and works as a noun or verb synonym for fear.

clue.text: Some of Veronese's paintings mounted in east end of church

indicators.note: in a down clue mounted means going upwards, so the letters read from bottom to top
some of means just part, so the letters are lifted from inside the words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of Veronese's and the start of paintings

explanation.surface: Some of the Renaissance painter Veronese's works are hung at the east end of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: Veronese was a Venetian painter of large religious canvases, which fits the church setting.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the semicircular recess, usually vaulted, at the eastern end of a church.

clue.text: Article in news strangely peters out

indicators.note: in places the article inside the jumbled news letters
strangely means in an odd way, so the letters of news are put in an odd order

parts.note: taken as written
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A story in the news gradually fizzles out, strangely enough.
explanation.walkthrough: NEWS is rearranged to WNES and A goes after the W.
explanation.definitionFit: To wane is to dwindle or decrease gradually, like the moon, so wanes means peters out.

clue.text: Instinctively ring home about spasmodic heart beat

parts.note: a ring is round like the letter O

indicators.note: about suggests turning round, so the home word is read backwards

parts.note: at home means in

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so only the middle letter of spasmodic is taken

parts.note: the fifth of the nine letters is central
a pulse is a regular beat

explanation.surface: A worried patient instinctively rings home about an irregular heartbeat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart beat' reads as one thing, but heart picks the middle letter of spasmodic and beat alone is the pulse.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something on impulse means acting suddenly without forethought, which is acting by instinct.

clue.text: Rest of soldiers given uniform in camp

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps

indicators.note: in tells us the uniform letter is put inside the camp word

parts.note: a camp is a side in a dispute
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Soldiers in camp are issued their uniforms and given some rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Camp' looks like a military base, but it is a faction in a dispute, as in the opposing camp.
explanation.definitionFit: A residue is what remains after the main part is gone, the remainder or rest.

clue.text: Notices doctor returning without drug and is furious

parts.note: to notice is to see

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the doctor abbreviation is read backwards
without in its old sense of outside, so the doctor letters sit around the drug

parts.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A patient spots the doctor coming back with no medicine and loses their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like lacking, but it is the old sense of outside: RD goes around E.
explanation.definitionFit: To see red is an idiom for becoming suddenly angry, like a bull charging a red cape.
